title: POC scoping: Benchmark harness integration - NexaHealth
summary: POC scoping call to align on benchmark goals for NexaHealth's conversational assistant POC. Discussed success criteria (latency p95, throughput), workload characteristics (tokens per turn, streaming usage), harness integration approach (customer scripts, k6/locust vs Redwood harness), test timelines, and security/VPC constraints. Agreed next steps: share harness repo + example scripts, run an initial dry-run with representative traces, and schedule a live load test next week.
next_steps: Liam to share Redwood benchmark-harness repo and sample scripts (2026-05-01)
Priya/Marco to provide 500 representative traces and token distribution by 2026-04-29
Schedule live load test with SE + customer on 2026-05-05
Sophie to confirm VPC & KMS details and provide firewall allowlist by 2026-05-03
action_items: Liam Chen - Share harness repo + sample streaming/non-streaming scripts - 2026-05-01
Tara Singh - Prepare initial benchmark config and recommended batch/kv-cache settings - 2026-05-04
Priya Patel - Export 500 representative chat traces and token histogram - 2026-04-29
Sophie Green - Send VPC peering and KMS contact + policy docs - 2026-05-03
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-25 09:23 PDT | Duration: 48 mins | Attendees: Liam Chen, Tara Singh (Redwood); Priya Patel, Marco Alvarez, Sophie Green, Evan Cho (NexaHealth)

[00:00] Liam Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Liam, AE on the account, Tara's our solutions engineer. we wanted to focus today on the benchmark plan and how we'll integrate your existing scripts into our harness.

[00:12] Priya Patel: Hi, thanks. couple of context points from our side — we're building a patient-facing assistant, right now prototype on our infra, latency is sensitive, we target p95 under 900 ms for simple queries and about 1.2s for multi-turn. throughput is modest but bursty, about 12 rps on peak. also most sessions use streaming because we do progressive UI updates.

[00:38] Marco Alvarez: yes and we have about 60k monthly active users, typical turn length is 30-75 tokens, occasionally 400-500 for long instructions. we can provide traces.

[00:50] Tara Singh: ok that helps. for benchmarking we usually need a token distribution, sample traces, and a decision on streaming vs non-streaming tests. streaming changes client-side measurements — end-to-end perceived latency will be earlier but server token throughput metrics differ.

[01:06] Evan Cho: quick q: when you say streaming benchmarks, do you mean chunked responses with server-sent events? because our client does websockets and expects partial tokens.

[01:15] Tara Singh: yeah chunked/streaming responses. our harness supports both modes: we can replay traces in a streaming mode that mimics your client and measure time-to-first-byte, ttf-token, and final-latency; and a non-streaming run where we measure single-request end-to-end and tokens/sec. both are useful.

[01:34] Priya Patel: perfect. what about load testing tools — we use k6 for load shapes. can we reuse those scripts?

[01:41] Liam Chen: absolutely. two common approaches: 1) you provide k6/locust scripts that hit the Redwood endpoint(s) and we run them from our infra to validate performance, or 2) we run our benchmark-harness which can ingest your trace JSON and replay at the exact timing and streaming cadence. if you'd like, we can take your k6 scripts and wrap them to call the harness or just run them as-is against a dedicated test endpoint.

[02:02] Marco Alvarez: we prefer option 2 since we want to keep the client behavior identical. how invasive is integrating our traces?

[02:09] Tara Singh: minimal — we accept newline-delimited trace records, each record should include the prompt, expected token count, and streaming flags. we'll provide an example. there might be minor noise from ASR or text normalization but that's fine.

[02:24] Sophie Green: security question: for a dedicated test instance, can we route through our VPC? we need to ensure no logs leave our tenancy and KMS is customer-managed.

[02:33] Liam Chen: yes for Dedicated or Private deployments we support VPC peering and customer-managed KMS. for hosted POC we can enable strict audit logs and retention policies, but for full isolation you'd probably want a Dedicated trial. we can provision a short-lived Dedicated pool scoped to your account for the load test.

[02:51] Sophie Green: ok and audit logs — do you expose request-level logs and redaction controls?

[02:56] Tara Singh: request-level logs are available in the console with RBAC, we also support redaction hooks and you can configure token-level retention. we'll share the security whitepaper and our SOC2 summary.

[03:07] Priya Patel: back to success criteria — besides p95 latency, we care about semantic stability across quantized model variants. can we run both FP16 and 4-bit quantized variants in the POC to compare throughput and quality?

[03:20] Tara Singh: yes, that's common. we'll define quality gating: we'll run a smaller eval suite for semantic pass/fail on a sample of prompts. if the quality delta exceeds your threshold (you can set e.g., <2% accuracy drop or hold on human eval), we won't promote the quantized variant.

[03:38] Marco Alvarez: what's the recommended sample size for evals tied to benchmarks? we want statistically meaningful results but quick iterations.

[03:45] Tara Singh: typically 200-500 prompts for initial gating. for production-level confidence we recommend 1k+. given your timelines we can start with 500 and expand.

[03:55] Evan Cho: timeline question — how long does it take to get a harness run and results back?

[03:59] Liam Chen: once we have traces and a test endpoint, an initial dry run takes a day, then a full load test + quality eval can be done in 2-3 days. end-to-end from traces to consolidated report about 4 business days.

[04:12] Priya Patel: sounds good. what about caching and kv cache — our workloads have short local context reuse, we expect significant wins if the cache is warm. how is that measured?

[04:21] Tara Singh: the harness can simulate warm vs cold KV cache runs. we usually do a warm-up phase where we replay prefixes to populate the cache, then run the load shape. instrumentation reports token-level latency and cache hit ratios. that helps estimate cost per request after cache effects.

[04:37] Marco Alvarez: and autoscaling behavior? we want to know how the Dedicated pool scales under bursty patterns.

[04:43] Liam Chen: for Dedicated we capture tail-latency under scale events and can model autoscale timings. we'll include a run with sudden load ramps to emulate your peak bursts. we can also provide guidance on config: min pool size to hit your 12 rps peak with p95 under target.

[04:58] Sophie Green: any compliance blockers for us to run tests? we have PHI in some traces — we need to ensure redaction before sharing or sign an NDA.

[05:06] Priya Patel: yes we'll scrub PHI before sending traces. we can sign the NDA, we'll coordinate offline.

[05:12] Liam Chen: noted. we'll send the security deck and an NDA link after the call.

[05:18] Tara Singh: small note on streaming metrics — measured by the harness as three things: time-to-first-byte, time-to-first-meaningful-token (we define heuristics), and final-latency. some clients consider ttfb most important. we can export these as csv and visualize in the console.

[05:34] Evan Cho: do you measure per-token cost estimates? we need cost per convo projection for finance.

[05:38] Tara Singh: yes token accounting is in the report; we can also run sensitivity analysis under different quantization and batching configs to show projected monthly cost.

[05:46] Priya Patel: ok quick recap — deliverables from Redwood: harness repo + examples, initial benchmark config, config suggestions for batching/quantization, security docs, and a proposed date for the live test. deliverables from NexaHealth: traces, k6 scripts (optional), confirmation on streaming behavior and PHI redaction.

[06:05] Liam Chen: exactly, and we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the load test on 2026-05-05 with Tara and an operations runbook.

[06:12] Marco Alvarez: one more question — does the harness support simulated network jitter? our mobile users see variable networks.

[06:18] Tara Singh: yes we can inject latency and jitter in the runner to measure perceived latencies. we'll add that to the config recommendations.

[06:25] Sophie Green: i'll work with Liam on the allowlist for IPs.

[06:29] Liam Chen: thanks everyone — we'll send the repo and a short checklist. any final q's?

[06:34] Priya Patel: nope, thanks all.

[06:36] Liam Chen: thanks, talk soon.

[06:38] End of transcript

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts — names sometimes misrecognized, a few dropped punctuation marks. Shared links mentioned: https://redwood.ai/benchmark-harness (example), security whitepaper (link to be shared), shared drive with traces (TBD).
